title: Judge the call, not the luck
principle: Judge a call by what you knew then, not the result.

screens.text: Let me start with a cricket story. It's the 2007 T20 World Cup final against Pakistan. Pakistan need 13 runs off the last over, with one wicket left. Harbhajan, the obvious choice, was hit for three sixes in his last over, so Dhoni throws the ball to Joginder Sharma.

screens.prompt: Joginder had played only a handful of games for India. Before I tell you what happened, what do you make of Dhoni's call?

options.label: A sensible choice, given his options
Can't tell until we see the result

screens.why: Here's what happened. The first ball was a wide, the second a swing and a miss, and the third a full toss that Misbah hit for six. Then, with six needed off four balls, Misbah tried a scoop, and Sreesanth caught it. India won by five runs, and the call became famous.

screens.prompt: Now imagine Misbah's scoop had gone for four, and Pakistan had won. Would that make Dhoni's call any worse?
screens.why: Exactly. Dhoni chose before the over began, and he knew the same things in both stories. Only where one ball landed has changed. The papers would have called it a blunder, but they'd have been judging the luck, not the thinking.

wrong.a: I see what you did: you judged the call by the final score. But Dhoni chose before the over began, and nothing he knew then had changed. Only where one ball landed was different.
wrong.c: I can see why you'd meet in the middle. But luck can't make a choice a little worse after it's made. Dhoni knew the same things either way, so it was the same call.

screens.title: Resulting
screens.text: Calling it a blunder would have been a trap. Think of two students: one copies and gets full marks, while another truly understands but slips once. Marks alone won't tell you who chose better. The poker player Annie Duke calls this trap resulting: judging a decision only by what happened.

screens.prompt: Let's go back to that final. To judge Dhoni fairly, which of these did he know when he chose?

items.text: Harbhajan had gone for three sixes
The first ball would be a wide
Joginder had closed out the semi-final
India would win by five runs

screens.why: Exactly. Start with what Dhoni knew when he chose. The wide, the scoop and the final score all came later. They tell you what happened, but they can't change how good his thinking was.

screens.title: Now it's your business
screens.text: Let's see if you can catch resulting yourself. Imagine you run a lunch tiffin service for offices. Every week you make calls like Dhoni's: which client to take, which cook to hire, which fair to spend money on. Some of your good calls will still go wrong.

screens.prompt: Let's try one. A fair stall costs ₹10,000, and 1 time in 4 it wins an order that leaves you ₹60,000. What's one fair worth?
screens.why: Well done. Spread the ₹60,000 win across four fairs and that's ₹15,000 a fair on average. Each fair costs ₹10,000, so you're left with ₹5,000 a fair. It's a good bet, even though most fairs bring no order.

wrong.a: I see what you did: ₹60,000 minus the ₹10,000 stall. But you win that ₹60,000 only 1 time in 4. Spread it across four fairs, that's ₹15,000 each, then take off the ₹10,000: ₹5,000.
wrong.c: That's what one losing fair costs, and you're right that most fairs lose. But the wins pay for the misses and more: ₹60,000 ÷ 4 is ₹15,000 a fair on average, and minus ₹10,000, that leaves ₹5,000.

screens.prompt: Here's where resulting bites. You miss 3 fairs in 4. How often will you go to two fairs in a row and win nothing?
screens.why: Exactly. ¾ × ¾ is 9/16, about 56 times in 100, so two empty fairs in a row are more likely than not. If you judged the bet after those two, you'd drop something that earns you ₹5,000 a fair on average.

wrong.a: That's the chance of two wins in a row: ¼ × ¼ = 1/16, about 6 in 100. Misses are the common case: ¾ × ¾ = 9/16, about 56 in 100.
wrong.b: I see what you did: you used one fair's chance of winning, 1 in 4. Missing once is ¾, and missing twice in a row is ¾ × ¾ = 9/16, about 56 times in 100.

screens.prompt: Now the other way round. You hired a cook without a trial day, and that month was your best ever. What's the lesson?

options.label: Keep the cook, but give the next one a trial
Skip trials from now on. It worked
The cook earned you that whole month

screens.why: Right. The good month doesn't prove that skipping the trial was smart, because the cook might have helped, or a festival, or a big new client. Keep the cook if they're good, but don't let one lucky month teach you a careless way to hire.

wrong.b: I see what you did: the month went well, so the method must be fine. That's resulting the other way round. You skipped the check and got lucky, so give the next cook a trial day.
wrong.c: Maybe, but a festival or a new office client could explain that month too. You can't tell from the result alone, so keep the cook if they're good, and give the next one a trial day.

screens.prompt: When a big call goes wrong, here's how to review it fairly. Put the steps in order.
steps: Write down what you knew then
Write down what you chose, and why
Ask: was it the thinking, or the luck?
Change your method only if the thinking was wrong
screens.why: Well done. You rebuild the decision as it looked at the time before you let the result in, and only then ask what it teaches you. That's how we judged Dhoni: what he knew first, the scoop afterwards.

screens.setup: Then one of your calls goes wrong. Before taking a new office client, you checked carefully: three good references and five years in business. Two months later it shuts down, owing you ₹36,000, and your partner says, 'No more new clients. Ever.'
screens.question: Was it a bad call, and what do you do now?

options.label: Agree. Only old clients from now on
options.outcome: You're safe for a while. Then two old offices move away, and with no new clients coming in, your kitchen runs half empty.
options.why: One bad result made you drop a sound method. That's resulting, and it shuts the door on every good client who came after.
options.better: Keep checking new clients, and ask them for the first month in advance.

options.label: Keep the checks, and ask new clients for a month's advance
options.outcome: New offices keep signing up. Each one pays its first month up front, so if one shuts down, you lose far less.
options.why: Well played. One failed client doesn't prove your checks were bad, so you keep them. But the loss did show you a risk you can shrink: how much you're owed before a new client pays.

options.label: Ignore it. Bad luck happens
options.outcome: You carry on exactly as before, so the next client who shuts down can leave you ₹36,000 short again.
options.why: You may be right that nobody could have seen the shutdown coming. But bad luck doesn't mean there's nothing to learn, and this loss showed you one thing you control: when new clients pay you.
options.better: Ask new clients for the first month in advance.

screens.text: Caught or four, Dhoni's call was the same. Judge a call by what you ___ then, not by the ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Dhoni had to choose with what he knew then, and whether Misbah's scoop was caught or went for four couldn't change that choice afterwards. Judge your own calls the same way: first ask what you knew, then ask what the result can teach you.

summary: Judge a decision by what you knew when you made it.
A good bet can lose many times in a row, so don't drop it after one miss.
Don't let the result rewrite the old call, but use it to fix what you can next time.

cards.front: You checked everything, and the deal still failed. Was it a bad decision?
options: Not if the thinking was sound
cards.back: Judge what you knew then. A good call can have a bad result.

cards.front: A bet wins 1 time in 4. How often do you lose twice in a row?
cards.back: ¾ × ¾ = 9/16. Losing streaks are normal on good bets.
